title: Tree: Preorder Traversal
directAnswer: Preorder = visit the Node first, then the Left subtree, then the Right subtree. Recursively it's three lines: visit, recurse left, recurse right. The iterative version uses a stack: push the root, then loop — pop and visit a node, push its RIGHT child first and its LEFT child second, so left is processed before right. Both are O(n) time; O(h) space. Preorder is the natural order for serializing or cloning a tree top-down.

remember.pattern: Depth-first traversal in Node → Left → Right order
remember.formula:
preorder(node):
    if node is null: return
    visit(node)
    preorder(node.left)
    preorder(node.right)
rules: Order is **Node, Left, Right** — the node is visited *before* either subtree.
Iterative: push **right child first, then left**, so the left is popped and processed first.
Preorder visits the root first, making it ideal for **serialization, cloning, and copying** top-down.
The base case (null → return) stops the recursion at the bottom of each branch.
Preorder of a BST is NOT sorted — only *inorder* gives sorted order.
whenToUse: Serializing or deep-copying a tree (you need the root before its children)
Building a prefix/Polish-notation representation of an expression tree
Any traversal where the parent must be processed before its descendants
antiSignals: You need sorted BST output → inorder, not preorder
You need children-before-parent (freeing nodes, postfix expressions) → postorder
You need level-by-level output → BFS level order
remember.takeaway: Preorder is the 'top-down' DFS: process a node, then its subtrees. The recursion is just the inorder code with the visit moved to the front. The iterative version's push-right-then-left ordering is the detail interviewers probe.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can produce preorder recursively and iteratively, and whether you get the stack push order right (right child before left).
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: In the iterative version, pushing the LEFT child before the right — which reverses the output so right subtrees come first.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Write the recursion instantly, then derive the stack version and explain WHY you push right before left (LIFO means the last pushed is popped first).

problemStatement: Given a pointer to the `root` of a binary tree, print the **preorder traversal** of the tree: the values visited in Node, Left-subtree, Right-subtree order, separated by spaces.
constraints: Output values are space-separated in preorder sequence
understanding: Produce the sequence of node values in Node → Left → Right order. We emit a node's value the instant we arrive at it, then descend into its left subtree fully, then its right subtree. The root is always first in the output.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I print the values or return a list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: HackerRank prints space-separated values. Returning a list is cleaner for testing in a general interview — confirm the expected output form.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Recursive or iterative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Recursive is the clean default. Offer the stack-based version if the interviewer asks to avoid recursion.

clarifyingQuestions.question: In the iterative version, which child do I push first?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Push the RIGHT child first, then the left. A stack is LIFO, so the left child (pushed last) is popped and processed first — matching Node, Left, Right.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is preorder of a BST sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Only inorder yields sorted order on a BST. Preorder is for top-down processing like serialization.

examples.explanation: Visit 4, then its left subtree (2, then 1, then 3), then its right subtree (5).
Visit 1, no left child, go right to 2, visit 2, then its left child 3.
Single node — just the node, no subtrees.

diagrams.title: When is the node visited?
diagrams.caption: Preorder visits the node before either subtree — the top-down DFS.

approaches.name: Recursive Preorder — Node, Left, Right
approaches.whenToMention: Start here. Three lines; just remember the visit comes first.
hints: Preorder means the node is processed before its subtrees. Where does the visit go relative to the two recursive calls?
Base case: a null node produces nothing → return.
For a real node: visit it, then recurse left, then recurse right. The visit is the very first action.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited exactly once with O(1) work → O(n) time. Recursion depth equals tree height h → O(h) space (O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed).
approaches.explanation:
Preorder is defined recursively: to traverse a node, visit it immediately, then fully traverse its left subtree, then its right subtree.

**Visit-first is the defining move.** The only difference between the three DFS traversals is where the visit sits among the two recursive calls. Putting it first — before recursing into either child — yields preorder, which always emits the root before anything below it.

**Why top-down matters.** Because a parent is always processed before its children, preorder is the order you want when each child's handling depends on the parent already existing: serializing a tree to a string, deep-copying it node by node, or writing an expression tree in prefix (Polish) notation. Reconstructing a tree from a preorder sequence is straightforward precisely because the root comes first.

**Base case.** A null pointer (the child of a leaf) has nothing to visit, so it returns and the recursion unwinds.

**Not sorted on a BST.** Unlike inorder, preorder on a BST is not sorted — it lists the root, then the entire smaller-than-root subtree, then the larger one. If you need sorted output, that's inorder.
approaches.insight: Preorder = inorder with the visit moved to the front. All three traversals are the same three statements reordered; preorder puts the visit first, giving you the parent before its descendants.

dryRun.intro: Emit each node on arrival, then go left, then right. Root is first.

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def preorder(root: Node) -> None:
    if root is None:                   # base case: nothing to visit
        return
    print(root.data, end=' ')          # 1) visit the node FIRST
    preorder(root.left)                # 2) left subtree
    preorder(root.right)               # 3) right subtree

java.explanation: Base case — null children produce no output.
Visit FIRST — this position is what makes it preorder (root before subtrees).

python.explanation: Visit before either recursion — the preorder position.

diagrams.caption: Visit order in parentheses: 4 first (root), then 2,1,3,5.

approaches.name: Iterative Preorder — Explicit Stack
approaches.whenToMention: Offer when recursion is discouraged. The push-right-then-left detail is the part interviewers test.
hints: Use a stack seeded with the root. What do you do each iteration to emit the root before its children?
Pop a node and visit it immediately (root-first). Then push its children so the LEFT is processed next.
A stack is LIFO: push the RIGHT child first, then the LEFT, so the left pops out before the right.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is pushed once and popped once → O(n) time. The stack holds at most O(h) nodes (right children waiting along the current path) — up to O(n) for a degenerate tree.
approaches.explanation:
Preorder visits the root first, which maps cleanly onto a stack: pop a node, visit it, and schedule its children for later.

**The push order is the whole trick.** A stack is last-in-first-out, so whatever you push *last* is popped *first*. We want the left child handled before the right, so we push the **right child first and the left child second**. On the next iteration the left child is on top and gets popped, visited, and expanded before the right subtree is ever touched.

**Why visit on pop.** Unlike inorder, there's no waiting: the moment we pop a node we can emit it, because preorder owes the node before its subtrees. After emitting, we push its children and move on.

**Guard against null children.** Only push children that exist; pushing nulls would force an extra null check on pop. The loop ends when the stack is empty, meaning every node has been visited.
approaches.insight: LIFO reverses push order, so to get Left-before-Right you push Right-before-Left. Saying that out loud — 'stack is LIFO, so I push the child I want last' — signals you understand the data structure, not just the recipe.

dryRun.intro: Pop-visit, then push right child then left child. Stack top is the rightmost in each row.

java.explanation: Seed the stack with the root so it's visited first.
Visit immediately on pop — preorder emits the node before its subtrees.
Push RIGHT first so it sits below the left on the stack.
Push LEFT last so it's on top and popped/processed before the right.

python.explanation: Left child pushed last → popped first (LIFO).

diagrams.title: Stack expansion order
diagrams.caption: Each pop visits a node and pushes right-then-left so left is handled next.

edgeCases.behavior: Each pop pushes only a left child → '3 2 1'.
Each pop pushes only a right child → '1 2 3'.

pitfalls: Pushing left before right — reverses subtree order in the output.
Pushing null children — forces an extra null check on every pop.
Visiting on push instead of pop — works for preorder but breaks if you later adapt this skeleton; visit-on-pop is the standard form.

commonMistakes: Confusing preorder with inorder by visiting after the left recursion.
In the iterative version, pushing the left child before the right.
Expecting preorder of a BST to be sorted — that's inorder.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong push order in the iterative version
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A stack is LIFO. Pushing the left child first means the right child is on top and gets processed before the left — reversing the intended order.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if (node.left != null) stack.push(node.left);
if (node.right != null) stack.push(node.right); // right ends up on top
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if (node.right != null) stack.push(node.right);
if (node.left != null) stack.push(node.left);   // left ends up on top

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Visiting after the left recursion (inorder by accident)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Preorder must emit the node before either subtree. Printing after recursing left produces inorder output instead.

patternNote: Preorder DFS (Node → Left → Right). One of three traversals differing only in visit position; preorder is top-down, emitting the root before its subtrees, which makes it the order for serialization and reconstruction. The iterative stack version hinges on pushing the right child before the left.
